prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We reconstruct lives in the intensive care unit, pieced together in a buffet dinner: two widows with cancerous breasts in their balled hands; a 30-year-old man in a three-month coma from a Buick and a brick wall; a woman who bleeds off and on from her gullet; a prominent socialite, our own nurse, shrieking for twins, “her bump gone”; the gallery of veterans, succored, awake, without valves, some lungs gone. Splicing the meats with fluids seasoned on the dressing room table, she sings “the bump gone” refrain in this 69-degree oven, unstuffing her twin yolks carved from the breast, the dark meat wrapped in tinfoil and clean newspaper; the half black registered nurse hums her six years in an orphanage, her adopted white family, breaded and primed in a posse, rising in clan for their dinner. We reload our brains as the cameras, the film overexposed in the x-ray light, locked with our double door light meters: race and sex spooled and rungs in a hobby; we take our bundle and go home.

In the intensive care unit, we assemble fragments of human stories as if arranging a buffet: two widows with breast cancer clutching their hands into fists; a thirty-year-old man who has been unconscious for three months after a Buick met a brick wall; a woman whose esophagus bleeds intermittently; a well-known society woman—one of our nurses—crying out for her twins, lamenting that “the bump” is gone; and a row of veterans, cared for and conscious, some missing valves, others missing parts of their lungs.

At the dressing-room table, while meat is cut and mixed with seasoned juices, she keeps singing the line about the vanished bump inside this room held at sixty-nine degrees. She empties out the twin yolks taken from the breast, with the dark meat folded in aluminum foil and clean newspaper. The registered nurse, half Black, softly recalls her six years in an orphanage and the white family that adopted her, all prepared and gathered like a band, rising together for their meal.

We reset our minds like cameras, though the film has been washed out by the glare of x-rays, our perceptions fixed behind double doors with their own measuring lights. Race and sex wind through the scene like reels and ladder rungs in a pastime. Then we gather up what is ours and leave for home.

The text portrays the intensive care unit as a space where shattered human lives and medical emergencies are pieced together through vivid, unsettling images. Rather than presenting the hospital as an orderly place of healing, the passage emphasizes fragmentation: bodies are injured, identities are reduced to symptoms, and personal histories appear only in brief, haunting glimpses. The intensive care unit becomes a setting where suffering is both intensely visible and strangely depersonalized.

Several patients and figures are evoked through short but powerful details. Cancer patients appear as part of the unit’s atmosphere of prolonged illness and physical decline. A comatose accident victim suggests sudden catastrophe and the fragile boundary between life and death. A bleeding woman introduces an image of immediate bodily crisis, while a grieving nurse reveals that suffering is not limited to patients alone. Injured veterans further expand the scene, connecting the hospital’s private pain to larger histories of violence, war, and social damage.

The speaker’s imagery blends surgery, food preparation, and bodily trauma, creating a disturbing sense of clinical and emotional dismemberment. Medical procedures are described in ways that resemble cutting, slicing, or preparing food, which makes the human body seem vulnerable and objectified. This overlap between the surgical and the domestic is unsettling because it turns care into something almost mechanical, even brutal. The result is a world in which bodies are opened, repaired, consumed by disease, or reduced to parts, while the emotional wholeness of the people involved remains difficult to recover.

Themes of race, gender, and identity also emerge throughout the passage. The depiction of a Black registered nurse is especially significant, as it draws attention to the racial and social identities of those who perform care within the hospital system. References to family, adoption, and social divisions suggest that the suffering witnessed in the intensive care unit cannot be separated from broader questions of belonging, inheritance, and inequality. The hospital becomes a place where biological vulnerability intersects with social identity.

Ultimately, the passage suggests both emotional overload and emotional detachment. The observers are confronted with an excess of pain: damaged bodies, grieving families, exhausted caregivers, and lives interrupted by illness or violence. Yet after witnessing these crises, they return home, implying a troubling separation between the world of suffering inside the hospital and the ordinary routines outside it. This movement away from the intensive care unit does not erase what has been seen; instead, it leaves behind a sense of numbness, unease, and unresolved grief.
outputs.L4:
The text presents the ICU as a place where human life is held together and taken apart at the same time. It is not shown as a clean, orderly space of recovery, but as a fragmented world of alarms, tubes, fluids, exposed skin, interrupted speech, and half-remembered histories. Patients appear not only as people with names and pasts, but also as bodies measured, opened, monitored, cleaned, fed, and rearranged by institutional routines. Their identities flicker between personhood and medical object: a chest becomes a site for intervention, a mouth becomes a tube, a pulse becomes a number on a screen. In this way, the ICU becomes both a sanctuary and a theater, a place where life is preserved through procedures that can also make the body seem less human.

The narrative moves through this world in a fractured, surreal style. Medical images merge with domestic and social images, especially the metaphor of the dinner table. Bodies are treated as if they are being served, consumed, displayed, or passed around for inspection. The language of eating and hospitality becomes unsettling when placed beside the language of surgery, diagnosis, and care. This creates a disturbing comparison between the patient’s body and a meal: something prepared, arranged, watched, and handled by others. The dinner table, normally associated with family, comfort, and community, is transformed into an operating table or hospital bed. Through this transformation, the text suggests that suffering can be turned into a kind of spectacle, something observed and processed by systems that claim to be humane but often depend on distance, control, and detachment.

The staff are also caught inside this machinery. Nurses, doctors, technicians, and other caregivers move through scenes of crisis with practiced efficiency, but they are not portrayed as untouched or invulnerable. Their work requires intimacy with pain, decay, and fear, yet it also demands emotional discipline. They must keep bodies alive while suppressing their own horror, fatigue, desire, grief, or anger. The text suggests that institutional care depends on this tension: the staff must be compassionate enough to respond to suffering, but detached enough to continue working. Over time, this creates its own trauma. The caregivers become witnesses to repeated emergencies and losses, absorbing the pain of others while being expected to function as part of a system.

The patients’ lives are not presented as isolated medical cases. Their illnesses intersect with histories of race, class, sexuality, gender, and social neglect. The ICU does not erase these differences; instead, it exposes them. Some bodies are more easily objectified than others. Some suffering is taken more seriously, while other suffering is dismissed, eroticized, racialized, or treated as inevitable. The hospital may appear neutral, but the text reveals that it is shaped by the same hierarchies that structure the outside world. Race and sex are not secondary details; they influence how bodies are seen, touched, described, feared, and valued. The clinical gaze is never purely clinical. It carries cultural assumptions and social histories into the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life.

Because of this, the ICU becomes a site where private pain and public power meet. A patient’s failing body is not only a biological fact, but also a record of exposure: to poverty, violence, discrimination, addiction, loneliness, labor, desire, and loss. The medical system tries to stabilize the immediate crisis, but it cannot fully address the conditions that produced or shaped that crisis. Machines breathe for patients, medications regulate blood pressure, and hands turn bodies to prevent wounds, yet these acts of care take place within a broader world that has already marked certain people as disposable. The text therefore presents medicine as both necessary and insufficient. It can save a life, but it cannot restore everything that has been taken.

The surreal collage form reflects this brokenness. Instead of offering a single, linear story, the text layers images and voices, allowing different narratives to collide. A clinical description may suddenly shift into memory, fantasy, racial commentary, sexual imagery, or mourning. This fragmentation mirrors the experience of trauma, in which events are not always remembered or understood in order. It also mirrors the ICU itself, where life is reduced to fragments: lab results, scans, charts, symptoms, family updates, whispered prayers, and the repetitive sounds of machines. The form refuses the comfort of a simple narrative of illness and recovery. Instead, it shows how suffering disrupts ordinary meaning.

At the center of the text is a deep concern with vulnerability. Every body in the ICU is breakable, dependent, and exposed. The patients are vulnerable because they cannot fully protect, explain, or control themselves. The staff are vulnerable because they must repeatedly confront the limits of their knowledge and power. Families are vulnerable because they must watch loved ones become unfamiliar, transformed by illness and technology. Even the institution is vulnerable, in a different sense, because its promise of control is constantly threatened by death, error, and the unpredictability of the body.

Yet the text does not simply condemn medical care. It recognizes that care is real, difficult, and often lifesaving. The problem is that care takes place within systems that can turn people into cases, bodies into objects, and suffering into procedure. The ICU preserves life, but it also reveals how easily life can be reduced to data, spectacle, or flesh. By combining medical imagery with scenes of consumption, racial and sexual tension, and overlapping stories of grief, the text exposes the contradictions of institutional care. It asks what it means to save a body without fully seeing the person inside it, and what it means to witness suffering in a society that has learned to organize, classify, and consume pain.

Ultimately, the text portrays the ICU as a haunting reflection of the larger world. It is a place where the most basic human facts—breathing, eating, touching, dying—become strange and charged with meaning. In its surreal and unsettling vision, the hospital is not separate from social life but an intensified version of it. There, the body becomes the place where medicine, power, race, sex, grief, and survival all converge. The result is a portrait of human beings at their most exposed: cared for and objectified, preserved and consumed, isolated and interconnected, fragile and still insistently alive.
outputs.L5:
**Buick and Splicing: Understanding Wiring Repairs in Buick Vehicles**

Buick vehicles are known for comfort, reliability, and refined design, but like any modern car, they depend heavily on electrical systems. From lighting and power windows to sensors, infotainment, and engine controls, wiring plays a major role in keeping a Buick operating properly. One common repair technique used in automotive electrical work is **splicing**.

Splicing refers to joining two or more wires together to restore or modify an electrical connection. In a Buick, splicing may be needed when a wire is damaged, corroded, cut, or replaced during a repair. For example, if a tail light harness, door wiring, or sensor connector becomes damaged, a technician may splice in a new section of wire instead of replacing the entire harness.

Proper splicing is important because poor connections can cause electrical problems such as flickering lights, warning messages, intermittent starting issues, or malfunctioning accessories. A good splice should be secure, protected from moisture, and matched to the correct wire gauge. Common methods include soldering and heat-shrink tubing or using high-quality crimp connectors designed for automotive use.

When working on a Buick, it is also important to follow wiring diagrams and disconnect the battery before making electrical repairs. Modern Buick models often include sensitive control modules, so incorrect splicing can lead to further problems or diagnostic trouble codes.

In short, splicing is a practical and often necessary technique in Buick electrical repair. When done correctly, it can restore reliable performance and extend the life of the vehicle’s wiring system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem set in an ICU that uses the language of film editing and a buffet dinner to reconstruct the lives of patients and nurses, with disturbing imagery around illness, race, sex, and motherhood.
counterfactuals.output:
In the ICU the night is spliced from blue light and broth: jump cut to a tray of gelatin trembling like a lung learning fear, match cut to a nurse’s gloved hand lifting the lid from a silver pan where steam rises with the faces of the intubated. The monitors provide the score—green arias, red percussion, the flat white hiss of oxygen dragged across the soundtrack. At the buffet of survival, everyone is served in portions: a widow’s pulse in a ramekin, a diabetic foot under cling film, the browned edges of a father’s name card, the soft rolls of morphine placed beside butter pats stamped with the hospital logo.

Here is Mrs. Alvarez, dissolved in close-up: rosary beads clicking like a projector, daughters on speakerphone orbiting her bed, their voices pixelated by distance and duty. Here is Mr. Greene, Black skin shining under antiseptic glare, his chart a montage of numbers that never learned to pronounce him, his body entered and entered by needles, bright doors, apologies. Here is the young nurse who ate cold pasta at 3 a.m. beside the supply closet, then wiped a stranger’s saliva from her wrist as tenderly as if bathing a child. Her own child sleeps at home in a crib filmed in absentia, a nursery rendered as B-roll: moon decal, unopened lotion, one sock under the radiator, the mother’s milk sealed in plastic bags like evidence.

The ventilators chew. The suction canisters bloom darkly. Behind each curtain, an alternate edit: a wedding reception where the groom’s hand shakes too much to hold champagne; a motel room where love was mistaken for hunger; a kitchen table where a son, pale with rage, learned the family recipe for silence. The nurses carry plates from bed to bed—ice chips, crushed pills in applesauce, pronouns, last rites, restraints. Their shoes squeak through the scene like bad Foley. They call each patient honey, sir, ma’am, baby, Mr. This, Ms. That, rebuilding dignity with the smallest available utensils.

At midnight the buffet opens wider. The catheter bags glow like weak tea. The wounds are garnished. A mother with a fever dreams she is carving herself into equal slices for her children; in the dream they line up politely with hospital trays, asking for the breast, the lullaby, the rent, the forgiveness. A man remembers a woman’s mouth and then only the red straw in his cup. A nurse adjusts his gown, not looking away from what life has made ridiculous and sacred. Desire, too, is edited here: censored, captioned, replaced by pressure sores, wedding rings taped to bed rails, the body’s old negotiations with shame.

Race enters not as metaphor but as paperwork, as the long shot of who gets believed, who gets restrained, whose pain arrives already suspect, whose daughter must speak in a sharper voice to summon the same mercy. The fluorescent lights do not confess. The camera does not confess. It merely pans over brown hands, white sheets, black monitors, yellow gowns, the whole ward color-corrected toward pallor.

By dawn, the charge nurse assembles the timeline: intake, decline, code, call, extubation, discharge, death. She drags each clip into place with invisible fingers. In the break room, scrambled eggs congeal beside fruit no one trusts. Someone has brought cupcakes, frosted pink for a baby shower postponed three times. The nurses eat standing up, mouths full of sugar and alarm. One laughs, then cries, then laughs again, a rough dissolve.

And still the beds keep asking to be mothers. They cradle the ruined and the newborn-old. They hold the incontinent, the furious, the beloved, the unnamed. They hold the nurses when the nurses lean briefly into their rails. In the final cut, no one leaves whole: each life is plated, sampled, wrapped in foil, sent down a corridor where the doors open and close like eyelids, where the credits roll backward into the body, where the feast goes on breathing through a tube.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental paragraph in the style of 1970s confessional/avant-garde poetry, blending hospital scenes, x-rays, coma patients, cancer, a missing pregnancy, and Thanksgiving-like food imagery into one unsettling collage.
counterfactuals.output: Under the hospital’s fluorescent harvest moon, the x-rays bloom like black chrysanthemums against the lightbox, each rib a wishbone snapped by strangers in gloves; down the hall the coma patients sleep through their own weather, mouths open as if waiting for cranberry sauce, for morphine, for a name to be ladled back into them. The oncologist carves the word malignant with the tenderness of a father at Thanksgiving, and I sit there holding my paper cup of ice chips, thinking of the pregnancy that vanished without ceremony—no cradle, no blood-stained announcement, only a white sheet tucked too tightly and the nurse saying sometimes the body reabsorbs its secrets. In the cafeteria, turkey sweats under plastic, gravy congeals like old plasma, sweet potatoes glow with the radioactive patience of tumors; everyone bows over their trays as if praying, while inside me the empty room keeps setting a place, keeps polishing the tiny fork, keeps asking what kind of mother forgets the guest who never arrived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a grotesque literary montage about intensive care patients and staff, where medical histories are “spliced” together like film reels and described through meat, dressing room, oven, and carving metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
In the intensive care unit the night is edited on a steel table.

The patients arrive as reels in dented canisters: Mr. Halvorsen, pneumonia with a side of old asbestos; Mrs. Kim, sepsis bloomed from a kidney stone; the boy from the overpass, pelvis shattered like a dropped platter; a woman whose heart keeps changing its mind. Their histories are not read but spliced—childhood asthma glued to factory dust, a wedding photograph stapled to cirrhosis, a long-ago bullet scar jump-cut into renal failure. The attending holds each strip of story to the light and watches the frames flicker: birthday cake, chest tube, Marlboro, ultrasound, snow shovel, ventilator. All of it runs through the projector of the body until the lamp burns hot and the film begins to curl.

Beds stand in rows like warming trays.

The patients are dressed for catastrophe. Paper gowns gape like bad costumes in a backstage corridor; socks are issued, bracelets tagged, wounds painted iodine-orange as if rouged for a part they never auditioned for. Nurses move among them with costume-room efficiency, pinning lines, untangling cords, changing soaked linens, fastening masks over mouths that have forgotten their lines. Here is a man powdered with talc and mottled blue beneath the jaw. Here is a woman zippered from sternum to navel, her incision neat as a theatrical seam. Here is a grandmother under a silver warming blanket, foiled like a roast not yet ready to be brought out.

The monitors applaud in green, arrhythmic light.

Somewhere a ventilator sighs and sighs, a mechanical oven breathing heat into loaves that will not rise. The room bakes in disinfectant and plastic: tubes softening in the warmth of palms, adhesive loosening at the edges, blood thickening in the catheter’s red straw. Fever turns foreheads glossy. Infection marinates in secret compartments. The pharmacists send up clear sauces in labeled bags—pressors, sedatives, antibiotics—dripping into the meat by the milliliter. Salt is chased. Potassium is corrected. Glucose is basted. The kidneys, those little drains in the kitchen floor, clog and overflow; dialysis is wheeled in like a chrome butcher’s cart.

At 3:12 a.m., a code is called.

Curtains are torn aside. The staff gather with carving tools: blades, paddles, syringes, laryngoscope shining like a silver tongue. The resident opens the mouth as though checking a stuffed bird for twine. The respiratory therapist threads the tube. The nurse counts compressions with the grim rhythm of a cleaver. Ribs crack softly, a sound everyone hears and no one keeps. Epinephrine goes in. Calcium. Bicarbonate. The body bucks once, then becomes a table again.

On the wall, the clock chews.

Between emergencies, the staff return to their stations carrying their own invisible charts. The charge nurse has a migraine folded behind one eye. The fellow’s father is dying in another hospital, in another gown, under another machine’s green weather. A new intern eats a protein bar over a trash can and tastes only gauze. They are spliced into the film too: coffee, divorce papers, gloved hands, a child’s missed recital, the sour locker-room smell of scrub tops worn too long. In the dressing room mirror of the medication alcove, they tie their masks and become necessary again.

Morning comes without mercy, a pale butcher unrolling its knives.

Rounds begin. Each bed is presented like a cut on a slab: age, diagnosis, overnight events, blood gas, urine output, prognosis. The team stands at the foot, carving the story into portions small enough to swallow. “Neuro unchanged.” “Pressor requirement down.” “Family meeting today.” “Poor candidate for surgery.” The words fall cleanly, professionally, though nothing in the room is clean except the instruments.

And still, inside the sealed heat of each body, old footage plays.

A girl learning to swim. A machinist coughing into his lunch pail. A mother buttering toast. A drunk turning a key. A heart attack in a supermarket aisle between apples and packaged meat. The reels jam, melt, resume. Scenes are cut and sutured, mislabeled, restored. The ICU keeps feeding them through: flesh into light, light into record, record into memory, until every life becomes a montage of what was saved, what was excised, and what the blade could not distinguish from the feast.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single paragraph of surrealist hospital prose involving widows with breast cancer, a man in a coma after a car crash, bleeding from the throat, a nurse who lost twins, veterans missing organs, and themes of race and adoption.
counterfactuals.output: In the hospital, night arrived wearing a paper gown and shuffled room to room, counting the widows with breast cancer as they floated above their beds like dark bouquets, each missing breast replaced by a small moon that hummed when the monitors blinked; down the hall, a man lay in a coma after a car crash, dreaming of highways that unspooled from his mouth while he bled from the throat in red ribbons the orderlies tried to fold into maps; the nurse who had lost twins carried two invisible infants in the crooks of her elbows and whispered their names into empty IV bags, which filled with rain; veterans missing organs sat upright in the ward like broken statues, their absent lungs, kidneys, and hearts ticking in jars beneath the nurses’ station, arguing softly about which country had claimed them first; and everywhere the fluorescent lights asked questions about race, about whose pain was believed, whose skin was mistaken for shadow, whose baby was placed in whose arms by adoption papers stamped with official blue birds, while the widows sang to the comatose man, the nurse rocked the air, and the hospital itself opened and closed like a wounded eye.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an ekphrastic, fragmented narrative that sounds like an overexposed documentary filmed in an ICU, mixing patient case notes with buffet-dinner imagery and ending with the observers taking their bundle home.
counterfactuals.output:
The film begins too white.

Not clean white—blown-out white, the kind that eats the edges of objects until the bedrails float, until the IV pole becomes a thin utensil in a banquet hall, until the patient’s face is less face than plate under a heat lamp.

**CASE NOTE 01:**  
Adult patient. Age obscured by glare. Admitted through night entrance. Respirations shallow, mechanically assisted. Skin cool. Family unavailable or not yet located. Wristband confirms name, though the camera refuses to focus.

A nurse leans into frame and her gloved hands flash like serving tongs.

There is a tray beside the bed: kidney basin, gauze, syringe caps, a folded blue drape. In the overexposure it resembles a buffet station after guests have passed through—crumbs of tape, curled plastic, the last pale sauces drying in disposable cups.

Someone says, “Pressure’s dropping.”

Someone else says, “Can you get another line?”

The monitor answers with its green arithmetic.

---

The documentary does not interview the patient.

Instead, it studies surfaces.

A forehead shining beneath adhesive.  
A mouth held open by tubing.  
The translucent yellow bag of fluids hanging like watered-down punch.  
A stack of blankets warming in a cabinet, dinner rolls under glass.

**CASE NOTE 02:**  
Sedation maintained. Pupils reactive. Abdomen distended. Bruising along flank. Unknown downtime. Labs pending. Continue vasopressors. Reassess.

The camera cuts, abruptly, to the family waiting room.

No family.

Only chairs upholstered in a pattern of small, polite leaves. A vending machine humming behind plexiglass. Coffee burned down to its bitter lacquer.

On a side table: cookies in a plastic clamshell, one missing. A paper napkin printed with festive fruit. Grapes, pineapple rings, strawberries glazed with impossible shine.

The observers stand near the doorway, not speaking. Their badges are turned inward. Their faces are filmed from the nose down: chins, masks, the fatigue around speech.

They watch the room as though it were evidence.

---

Back in the ICU, the ceiling lights bloom.

Everything blooms.

The patient’s chest rises under the sheet with the slow insistence of dough proofing beneath a towel.

A respiratory therapist adjusts the ventilator and the machine exhales in measured servings.

**CASE NOTE 03:**  
Vent settings modified. Oxygen requirement increased. Secretions thick. Suction performed. Patient tolerated procedure poorly. Saturation recovered to 91%.

The suction canister fills with amber-pink fluid. The lens lingers too long. It has the horrible gloss of carving juices collected beneath roast meat.

No one says this.

Medicine depends on not saying this.

Instead: “Clamp.”  
Instead: “Flush.”  
Instead: “Again.”  
Instead: “Hold pressure.”

A metal cart rolls in, rattling faintly, bearing instruments in sterile paper. It could be dessert service. It could be a tray of silverware wrapped for a wedding.

The nurse tears open the packets with practiced elegance.

---

The documentary voiceover arrives late, as if embarrassed.

It tells us the unit contains twelve beds. It tells us the average length of stay. It tells us about staffing ratios, alarm fatigue, the ethics of intervention. It tells us, in a calm public-television voice, that the human body under stress becomes a system of priorities.

Heart before hand.  
Air before name.  
Blood before story.

But the images keep misbehaving.

The pressure bag is a swollen wineskin.  
The medication labels are place cards.  
The sterile field is a tablecloth laid for guests who may not arrive.

**CASE NOTE 04:**  
Nutrition: NPO.  
Fluids: ongoing.  
Output: minimal.  
Code status: full.  
Prognosis: guarded.

Guarded, the note says.

As if prognosis were a door.

As if someone were standing behind it with a tray.

---

At 19:00 the shift changes.

The departing team gives report in a low murmur. The incoming team receives the patient in fragments, the way one receives leftovers: sealed containers, labels, times, warnings about what has spoiled.

“Admitted hypotensive.”  
“Two liters in.”  
“Scan showed—”  
“Family still not reached.”  
“Watch the potassium.”  
“Don’t trust the cuff pressure.”  
“Responds to pain, maybe.”

The patient does not respond to the handoff.

The patient is handed off anyway.

In the staff room, under fluorescent mercy, someone has brought food. Aluminum pans under foil. A tray of cut fruit sweating into itself. Pasta thickening in a lukewarm sauce. Rolls pressed together in a soft, obedient row.

The camera does not let the workers eat in peace.

It watches forks scrape paper plates. It watches a resident pour salad dressing into the corner of a container. It watches a nurse standing, chewing quickly, pager clipped at the hip like a small impatient animal.

A sign taped above the sink reads:

PLEASE LABEL YOUR FOOD  
UNLABELED ITEMS WILL BE DISCARDED FRIDAY

---

**CASE NOTE 05:**  
Patient remains unstable. Skin mottling noted at knees. Lactate elevated. Continue current management. Awaiting consult. Awaiting family. Awaiting response.

Awaiting is the main intervention.

The observers return to Bed 7.

They have been present since morning, perhaps longer. Their purpose is unclear. Quality review, ethics, training, film crew, angels—the documentary refuses to identify them. They stand just beyond the curtain, holding clipboards or prayer books or nothing.

One observes the monitor.  
One observes the hands.  
One observes the sheet where it rises and falls.  
One observes the small bundle of belongings sealed in a clear plastic bag: socks, a ring, a cracked phone, a shirt cut open from collar to hem.

The bag rests on the counter beside specimen cups and unused tape.

Personal effects.

The phrase appears onscreen.

PERSONAL EFFECTS.

Then the image blows out again, so violently that the letters dissolve.

---

Night thickens outside the sealed windows.

Inside, there is no night, only levels of brightness.

The patient’s body becomes a landscape of access points: neck, arm, wrist, groin. Tubes enter and leave. Clear liquids go in. Dark liquids come out. Numbers climb, fall, blink, correct themselves, lie.

The buffet in the staff room is reduced to remnants.

One spoon abandoned in beans.  
One lemon wedge hardened at the rind.  
Fruit collapsing into syrup.  
Foil crumpled like emergency blankets after use.

**CASE NOTE 06:**  
No significant neurological improvement. Blood pressure supported pharmacologically. Family contacted at 22:14. En route. Continue monitoring.

But the family does not appear in the film.

Or if they do, they are only coats in the hallway, hands over mouths, an intake of breath cut before sound.

The observers gather closer.

The camera trembles for the first time.

The ventilator keeps carving the air into portions.

---

Morning, or what passes for it, returns as a whiter white.

The patient is quieter now, though the room is not.

A physician removes their glasses and rubs the bridge of their nose. A nurse smooths the sheet. Someone silences an alarm before it finishes asking its question.

**CASE NOTE 07:**  
Condition unchanged. Goals-of-care discussion documented. Comfort measures considered. Pending decision.

The food is gone from the staff room.

The pans have been stacked, scraped, rinsed. The table is wiped clean except for one translucent smear no one noticed. A trash bag sags with plates, cups, napkins, evidence of appetite.

In Bed 7, the sheet is drawn higher.

The patient’s belongings remain in the plastic bag.

The observers stand around it now.

Not the body.

The bundle.

Socks nested together. Phone dark. Shirt folded as well as a severed shirt can be folded. Ring in a small envelope, labeled. Everything reduced, preserved, transferable.

One observer lifts the bag.

The plastic crackles loudly in the overexposed room.

For a moment it looks like a parcel from the buffet table: something saved for later, wrapped carefully, carried out after the lights come up and the guests have stopped pretending they are hungry.

No voiceover explains.

No note completes the chart.

The observers sign a line, tuck the bundle beneath an arm, pass through the sliding doors into the bleached corridor, and take it home.
